output:
**An open letter about the pier and buoy temperatures**

Several people have emailed asking why my pier logger reads warmer than the offshore buoy. It’s a fair question: the October means were **15.9°C at the pier and 14.1°C at the buoy**, a difference of about **1.8°C**. In winter, that gap shrinks to roughly **0.4°C**.

The instruments are measuring different places, at different depths. My logger is strapped to a piling at 3 metres, about 150 metres from shore. The buoy is roughly 25 kilometres offshore, with its sensor just below the surface over deep water. We shouldn’t expect those readings to match.

Shallow nearshore water warms in the sun, and the bay is sheltered from some of the upwelling that keeps offshore water cold. One reader sent a genuinely helpful screenshot overlaying the two records: the gap tracks sunny afternoons. That pattern, together with the smaller winter difference, points to real oceanography rather than a faulty instrument. Sensor depth also matters, so this isn’t a perfectly controlled comparison of nearshore and offshore conditions.

I do check the logger. It records every 10 minutes; I retrieve and download it every six weeks and replace the battery annually. My two-point calibration check uses an ice bath and a room-temperature bath, compared against a laboratory reference thermometer. At the last check, in September 2026, the measured offset was **+0.12°C**, well inside specification and far too small to explain the October gap.

Fouling is worth checking, too. In August, I retrieved the logger with a barnacle colony and a decorator crab living on the housing. I scraped it clean; the readings didn’t change.

Neither record is “the” temperature of Monterey’s coastal water. They answer different questions. If you’re diving the breakwater, the pier logger is the more relevant number—though conditions can still vary with depth, tide and location.

Thanks to everyone who has asked questions or compared records. Please email me if you’d like the raw CSV and want to take a closer look.
